title: Lincoln's Letter to General Hooker
text:
In January 1863, after the Union defeat at Fredericksburg, Abraham Lincoln removed Ambrose Burnside from command of the Army of the Potomac and gave the post to Joseph Hooker. Hooker was a capable, aggressive general, but he had openly criticized Burnside and undermined him, and he had been heard saying that the country needed a dictator.

On January 26 Lincoln wrote to Hooker. He began by saying he had appointed him for good reasons, but that there were things about him he was not satisfied with. He listed his strengths frankly: Lincoln believed him a brave and skillful soldier, who kept politics out of his profession and had confidence in himself. Ambition within reasonable bounds did good rather than harm. But under Burnside, Lincoln wrote, Hooker had taken counsel of his ambition and thwarted his commander, doing a great wrong to the country and to an honorable brother officer.

Then came the famous lines: "Only those generals who gain successes, can set up dictators. What I now ask of you is military success, and I will risk the dictatorship." He closed by telling him to beware of rashness, but to go forward with energy and sleepless vigilance and give the country victories.

Hooker was defeated at Chancellorsville that May.
lesson: Tell people plainly what you value in them and what worries you, in the same conversation. Clear expectations respect both the person and the task.
source: Lincoln to Joseph Hooker, January 26, 1863, Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, Volume 6
